title: The Saka Era Begins Its Long Clock

title_i18n.en: The Saka Era Begins Its Long Clock

subtitle: How a Satrap’s Count of Years Became India’s Quiet Clock
era: Saka era epoch, 78 CE and later use
moral: A date can outlive the throne that first counted it.

sources.citation: Andhau inscriptions dated in years 11 and 52 of the Saka era, in D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, vol. 1, 1965
sources.note: Primary dated evidence anchoring Chashtana's reign in the Saka era.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy, Oxford University Press, 1998, pp. 182-184
sources.note: Summarizes the Saka era controversy and epigraphic usage.

sources.citation: Harry Falk, The yuga of Sphujiddhvaja and the era of the Kushanas, Silk Road Art and Archaeology 7, 2001
sources.note: Important recent redating that weakens older identifications of Kanishka with the 78 CE era.

panels.shot: low-angle dramatic wide of a stone inscription glowing against a starry sky, numbers etched deep while Chashtana’s silhouette looms behind

dialogue.text: In 78 CE, a satrap named Chashtana began to count his years—and that count still beats, unseen, inside India’s national calendar.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye over western India, sweeping from desert coast to inland city

dialogue.text: Western India, first century of the Common Era—ports at Kutch, caravans over salt plains, and inland cities like Ujjain humming with trade and ritual time.

panels.shot: mid-shot of Chashtana in a council hall, lit by oil lamps

dialogue.text: Here ruled the Western Kshatrapas, Saka satraps of foreign steppe stock, now long rooted in this land; among them rose Chashtana, son of Ghsamotika.

panels.shot: close-up on Chashtana studying coins and tablets

dialogue.text: He ruled not with mythic thunder, but with metal, record and tax; his power flowed through coins, land-grants and dates scratched into stone.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot as Chashtana looks at priests and scribes arguing before him

dialogue.text: Across his realm, dates clashed—old local eras, regnal counts, lunar months, Greek-style reckonings brought by earlier kings.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Chashtana in thought, light catching one eye

dialogue.speaker: chashtana
dialogue.text: If my writ is to hold, our years must march as one.

panels.shot: symbolic montage wide, calendar glyphs overlaying his figure

dialogue.text: Some scholars see his answer in a decision: to root his rule in a single era, a new count of years beginning around 78 CE.

panels.shot: close-up on a stonecutter’s hands carving numerals into rock

dialogue.text: The modern name is the Saka era. Its year one is fixed by today’s scholars in 78 CE, though the hand that first began it remains debated.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Kutch landscape with an inscription pillar at Andhau

dialogue.text: Out at Andhau in Kutch, in this dry country under his sway, two silent stones still bear its ticking years.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on the inscription text band where the date appears

dialogue.text: One speaks of year 11 of the Saka era; another, year 52. D. C. Sircar read these numbers as anchors for Chashtana and his line.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide of a satrapal court scene dissolving between rulers

dialogue.text: Long after his own name fades from many records, Western Kshatrapa grants and coin legends keep using this Saka count, year after year.

panels.shot: split-panel style composition, one side showing a Kushan court, the other a scholar’s desk

dialogue.text: Earlier, many tied this era to Kanishka of the Kushans, seeing his rise as the dawn of 78 CE; recent work, like Harry Falk’s, has loosened that bond.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar turning pages of an epigraphic corpus

dialogue.text: Richard Salomon and others follow the inscriptions themselves: where a date says ‘of the Saka era,’ they track how, where and by which rulers it was used.

panels.shot: montage of different inscriptions from western India, their date lines highlighted

dialogue.text: Across centuries, from these satraps onward, inscriptions in western India quietly mark time ‘by the Saka era,’ even as dynasties rise and fall around them.

panels.shot: contrast panel showing a bard reciting to a king with imagined heroic scenes behind him

dialogue.text: Meanwhile, storytellers spin new cycles—Vikramaditya, Shalivahana, heroic foes of ‘Sakas’—weaving the era into legend, but these tales rest in poetry, not in stone dates.

panels.shot: modern cityscape of New Delhi with a subtle overlay of calendar pages

dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, an independent India chooses this same Saka era for its national civil calendar, setting year one at 78 CE once more before the world.

panels.shot: close-up of a printed Indian national calendar page showing Saka year alongside CE

dialogue.text: Every time those twin dates are printed—a Saka year beside a Common Era one—the long clock that began in 78 CE ticks again, half-seen yet precise.

panels.shot: ghostly overlay of Chashtana’s face over the modern calendar and inscription

dialogue.text: We may never prove whose mind first fixed that epoch, but Chashtana’s age shows how a ruler’s need for order can cast a shadow longer than any throne.
